summary: This is a multicenter, open-label, Phase I study designed to evaluate the safety, tolerability, efficacy, and pharmacokinetic /pharmacodynamic characteristics of SIM0518 in trial participants with ALK-positive or ROS1-positive locally advanced or metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC). The study starts with a dose escalation part (Part 1), followed by a dose expansion part (Part 2). A Drug-Drug Interaction (DDI) study (Part 3) may be conducted after the Recommended Dose of SIM0518 is determined.

title: Development and Validation of a Gene Expression-Based Prognostic Model for Patients With Small Cell Lung Cancer Treated With Chemotherapy.
authors: Liu T, Zhou T, Mo S et al.
abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) remains one of the most aggressive malignancies, with limited tools for predicting outcomes and guiding treatment. We developed an SCLC-Predictive Risk Score (PRS) model for patients treated with chemotherapy using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression. The model comprised five genes and was developed in a training cohort of 50 patients using an innovative 795-gene panel of tumor- and immune-related genes analyzed on the NanoString nCounter platform. Gene expression was measured in routine clinical formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded SCLC specimens, predominantly puncture specimens (36/50). The SCLC-PRS model stratified patients into high-risk (PRS-H) and low-risk (PRS-L) groups; patients in the PRS-H group had significantly worse overall survival (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.35, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.18-0.69; p = 0.002) and progression-free survival (HR = 0.44, 95% CI: 0.23-0.84; p = 0.008). The prognostic performance of the model was externally validated in two independent cohorts (GSE60052, n = 38; George cohort, n = 47). Multivariate Cox analysis confirmed SCLC-PRS as an independent prognostic factor. PRS-L tumors exhibit a favorable tumor immune microenvironment, with increased CD45+ immune infiltration, reduced Tregs or exhausted CD8+ T cells, and upregulated antigen presentation (MHC-I/II). Overall, the SCLC-PRS model is an innovative, cross-platform-compatible, and clinically applicable prognostic tool with potential utility for risk stratification and personalized treatment.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors in Driver-Negative Stage IV Non-small Cell Lung Cancer Patients Receiving Thoracic Radiotherapy: A Single-Center Retrospective Study.
authors: Shang C, Yang J, Wang M et al.
abstract: IntroductionThe role of thoracic radiotherapy (TRT) in stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) without targetable driver alterations remains unclear. We evaluated outcomes, prognostic factors, and safety in patients receiving TRT and systemic therapy.MethodsIn this single-center retrospective cohort study, we analyzed patients identified according to predefined criteria who received TRT and systemic therapy at a single tertiary cancer center between January 2019 and December 2023. Overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and local control (LC) were estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Conventional Cox regression constituted the primary prognostic analysis, with Firth penalized Cox regression used as a small-sample sensitivity analysis. Exploratory conditional landmark and time-dependent Cox analyses assessed potential time-related bias.ResultsForty-eight patients were included. Median OS, PFS, and LC were 33.17 months (95% CI 19.29-47.05), 12.17 months (95% CI 8.89-15.45), and 12.47 months (95% CI 9.00-15.98), respectively. Best in-field response was partial response in 12 patients (25.0%), stable disease in 32 (66.7%), and progressive disease in 4 (8.3%). Squamous histology was consistently associated with poorer OS and PFS, whereas other multivariable associations were less stable in sensitivity analyses. Time-dependent anti-PD-1 exposure was not significantly associated with OS. Metastatic progression predominated among patients who died. In the exploratory 6-month conditional landmark analysis, TRT timing was not associated with OS or PFS. Grade 3-4 pneumonitis and esophagitis each occurred in one patient (2.1%), and no grade 5 adverse event was documented.ConclusionMost irradiated thoracic lesions showed partial response or stable disease at the best post-TRT assessment, while distant progression predominated among patients who died during follow-up. The prognostic findings are exploratory and require validation in larger prospective cohorts.

title: Safety and Efficacy of Reduced-Dose Stereotactic Radiosurgery Dose Administered With Concomitant Central Nervous System-Penetrant Systemic Therapy for Brain Metastases.
authors: McClelland S
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: The reported rate of symptomatic radiation necrosis (SRN) in patients with brain metastases treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy and concomitant single-fraction stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is as high as 20%. Previous work has piloted reduced-dose SRS as a potential solution. We present our experience with reduced-dose SRS to further assess its safety and efficacy for this patient population.
METHODS: Patients receiving SRS within 30 days of CNS-penetrant systemic therapy for brain metastases of 0 to 2 cm maximum diameter on MRI were treated with 18 Gy SRS and prospectively followed. The rates of 6-month local control and 6-month SRN were assessed.
RESULTS: Fifty-nine brain metastases were treated in 17 patients. The most common systemic therapy used was single-agent atezolizumab (25% of lesions) and single-agent pembrolizumab (19% of lesions). The most common primary tumors were small cell lung cancer, renal cell carcinoma, and lung adenocarcinoma (68% of lesions). The 6-month local control rate was 96%, with no 6-month SRN.
CONCLUSIONS: In the largest series examining reduced-dose SRS with concomitant CNS-penetrant systemic therapy, our findings confirm previous reports of the safety and efficacy of single-fraction 18 Gy SRS for brain metastases with maximum diameter 0 to 2 cm receiving therapy within 30 days of SRS. The excellent local control with minimal SRN at this dose supports 18 Gy for patients with brain metastases 2 cm or smaller receiving CNS-penetrant systemic therapy as preferable to the traditionally higher SRS doses, which have represented the standard of care, while remaining preferable to systemic therapy alone.

title: Associations of Tumor Proximity to the Intersegmental Plane and Segmental Bronchial Orifice with Insufficient Surgical Margins during Segmentectomy for Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Japanese Single-Center Retrospective Study.
authors: Mori H, Yanagihara T, Kikuchi S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Achieving an adequate surgical margin is a key oncological consideration during segmentectomy for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This study aimed to determine whether anatomical distance parameters measured on computed tomography (CT) were associated with insufficient surgical margins.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 151 patients with NSCLC who underwent segmentectomy or subsegmentectomy between 2012 and 2025. Tumor location was quantified on preoperative CT using the distance from the tumor to the intersegmental plane (Distance-ISP) and the bronchus-to-tumor distance (BTD). Factors associated with an insufficient pathological margin (≤10 mm) were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: The median age was 71 years, and the median pathological tumor size was 20 mm. An insufficient pathological margin (≤10 mm) was observed in 90 of 151 patients (59.6%). In the multivariable analysis, shorter Distance-ISP remained independently associated with an insufficient margin (odds ratio [OR], 1.18 per 5-mm decrease; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.04-1.34; p=0.009). The association for shorter BTD was in the same direction but was not statistically significant (OR, 1.10 per 5-mm decrease; 95% CI, 0.98-1.24; p=0.118).
CONCLUSION: Shorter Distance-ISP was independently associated with an increased likelihood of an insufficient surgical margin, whereas the independent association with BTD was not confirmed. Assessing both anatomical parameters may provide complementary information for preoperative surgical planning.

title: A multimode radiobiological model for advanced radiation therapy.
authors: Ma CC
abstract: Reliable radiobiological modeling is essential to the consistent dosimetric analysis and outcome comparison between conventionally fractionated radiation therapy (CFRT) that employs small daily doses (1.8-4Gy) and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) that employs large daily doses (> 5Gy). This work investigates a new radiobiological model, the multimode (MM) model, for both CFRT and SBRT.The MM model assumes the existence of different modes of cell killing because of unsuccessfully repaired radiation damage to the cell DNA by any number of ionization events (or radiation tracks). The validity of the multimode model was tested using previously published survival fractions of various cell lines. A comparison of the goodness-of-fit of the linear quadratic (LQ), multitarget (MT), universal survival curve (USC) and MM models was made to the survival curve of 12 non-small-cell lung cancer cell line. The same agreement was obtained between the USC and MM models with the survival data, which was significantly better than that with the LQ and MT models. The multimode model is a comprehensive model that may offer a superior description of the mammalian cell survival curve in both conventional and ablative dose ranges, which can be used for designing new fractionation schemes and predicting and understanding treatment outcomes for both CFRT and SBRT.

title: Promoter CpG island hypomethylation and overexpression of molecules homologous to the muscle autoantigens acetylcholine receptor and ryanodine receptor in thymoma epithelial cells associated with myasthenia gravis.
authors: Hong Y, Li HF, Guo Y et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thymoma-associated myasthenia gravis (TAMG) represents the paraneoplastic subtype of MG and is characterized by autoantibodies against skeletal muscle proteins, such as acetylcholine receptor (AChR), titin, and ryanodine receptor (RyR). Thymic epithelial cells of TAMG patients overexpress neuronal and neuromuscular genes that code for MG autoantigen epitopes. This may contribute to the autoimmune breakdown in TAMG patients. This study explored whether such aberrant expression of autoimmune epitopes is regulated by their promoter CpG methylation profiles.
METHODS: The thymoma bulk RNA sequencing, single cell RNA sequencing, and DNA methylation data were collected from 40 TAMG and 96 non-MG thymoma patients using three independent cohorts. A novel algorithm using a multiple linear regression model was developed to examine the gene promoter CpG island methylation status in TAMG and non-thymoma MG patients. The correlation between promoter CpG island and RNA expression in the TAMG thymoma was explored.
RESULTS: In both TAMG and non-MG thymoma, the global promoter CpG islands were hypomethylated and were negatively correlated with RNA expression. The CpG islands at promoters of muscle-like epitope genes, NEFM and RYR3, were significantly hypomethylated in TAMG thymoma and negatively correlated with mRNA expression in both a primary and a verification cohort. For MG antigen genes CHRNA1, TTN and RyR1, the CHRNA1 promoter CpG site methylation correlated negatively with CHRNA1 RNA expression. However, there was no difference in promoter methylation status between TAMG and non-MG thymomas. For the AIRE gene, the promoter CPG islands were significantly hypermethylated and negatively correlated with mRNA expression. Both bulk and single cell RNA sequencing showed that key genes involved in the DNA CpG methylation pathways, including DNMT1, UHRF1 and HDAC1, had a reduced expression in thymic epithelial cells of TAMG thymoma.
CONCLUSIONS: Our results indicate that the aberrant overexpression of muscle-like epitopes in TAMG might be driven by CpG island hypomethylation. This represents a novel mechanism for intrathymic autoantigen regulation, relevant for the early pathogenesis of TAMG and thymoma-associated autoimmune disorders. Our findings should be verified in larger cohorts and with functional and histological validation.

title: Anti-TGFβ peptide P144 augments CAR-T cell efficacy through neutrophil recruitment and TME remodeling in malignant mesothelioma
summary: Malignant mesothelioma is a rare, aggressive and highly desmoplastic cancer characterised by a profoundly immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME). Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematological malignancies, but its activity against solid tumours such as mesothelioma remains limited, in part through transforming growth factor-beta (TGF{beta})-mediated immunosuppression. To address this barrier, we engineered murine CAR-T cells that simultaneously target tumour antigen and deliver TGF{beta} blockade to the tumour. We first compared two anti-TGF{beta} peptides, the beta glycan-derived P144 and the phage-display-derived P17, in vitro; both attenuated TGF{beta}-induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and reporter activity, but P144 suppressed canonical Smad3 phosphorylation more effectively and was selected for downstream work. Murine CAR constructs targeting either mesothelin (M11) or fibroblast activation protein (FAP) were modified to secrete P144, and the resulting products were assessed in co-culture assays and in the syngeneic AE17m model of mesothelioma. P144 secretion did not alter transduction efficiency, expansion or antigen-specific cytotoxicity, but markedly increased antigen-driven IFN{gamma} production, most notably at low effector-to-target ratios.
